title: Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard -- Ch. 4: Chief Justice Davide: An Introduction
keywords: Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard
Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr.
introduction of a guest of honor
primary_topics: Chapter 4 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' -- the speech introducing Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. as guest of honor, deliberately setting aside the biography the media had already published in order to present the man CJP knew from three years of sitting with him.
A portrait of Davide's personal character: simple, transparent, abstemious, humble and soft-spoken yet self-actualized, with no craving for money because he is rich in what money cannot buy.
The two qualities CJP singles out as standing out in Davide's character as a jurist -- his thoroughness and his moral courage -- each developed in turn.
The argument that moral courage is to a magistrate what political will is to a sovereign head, and that without it a judge who knows every statute and charter by heart is really nothing.
sub_topics: The six biographical facts the broadcast and print media had already heralded -- Cebu schooling and a UP law degree; election as an opposition member of the Batasang Pambansa; membership in both the 1971 Constitutional Convention and the 1986 Constitutional Commission; service as Comelec chair and head of the fact-finding commission on the 1989 coup attempt; his marriage to Virginia Jimenea-Perez and their five children; and his 95-year old father's tears of joy.

CJP's decision not to repeat those facts but to introduce the speaker as he had known him during three years together in the Court, in en banc meetings and in the Third and First Divisions Davide chaired.
Davide's simple and transparent way of life: he does not drink, smoke or gamble, rarely attends social occasions outside official functions, and favors brisk early-morning walking.
His humility and self-knowledge -- aware of what he can and cannot do, with a vision of what needs doing and a clear concept of how to accomplish it.
First quality, thoroughness: ponencias loaded with relevant details, avid and fast reading, waking at 3:30 a.m., arriving at the Court by 6:30 a.m. and working ceaselessly until evening.
Thoroughness as memory too -- recalling what was discussed or agreed in the past, and quoting from memory footnotes and asides from CJP's own ponencias during a deliberation.

Second quality, moral courage, set against the lack of political will criticized in elected policymakers: the willingness to battle the establishment, to be a beacon for the weak and to stand for conviction against all odds.
Moral courage as resting on a purity of spirit and clarity of conscience -- only one with integrity beyond suspicion and no skeletons to hide can afford to challenge the gods.
The closing turn that the guest has not only challenged the gods but has himself become the loftiest of the Olympian "gods of Padre Faura," before naming him as Chief Justice of the Republic.
signature_phrases: he is humble and soft-spoken, almost self-deprecating but at the same time self-actualized
he has been blessed with an abundance of the things that money cannot buy
a gluttonous appetite for the minutiae of judicial work
He dissects issues with a surgeon's scalpel and moves his pen with laser-like precision

the loftiest of the Olympian "gods of Padre Faura."

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' reproduced the speech with which Justice Panganiban introduced Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. as guest of honor. He began by listing the six biographical facts the broadcast and print media had already heralded -- Davide's Cebu schooling and law degree from the University of the Philippines; his election as an opposition member of the Batasang Pambansa during the Marcos years; his membership in both the 1971 Constitutional Convention and the 1986 Constitutional Commission, making him a seasoned constitutionalist; his service as Comelec chair and as head of the commission that investigated the almost-successful 1989 coup attempt; his marriage to Virginia Jimenea-Perez and their five children; and the tears of joy of his 95-year old father -- and then declined to repeat them, choosing instead to introduce the speaker as he had known him during three years together in the Court, in en banc meetings and in the Third and First Divisions Davide chaired. He described a man who lives simply and transparently, who does not drink, smoke or gamble, rarely attends social occasions outside official functions, walks briskly in the early morning, and is humble and soft-spoken yet self-actualized, with no craving for money because he is rich in integrity, wisdom, humility, patriotism and a sense of righteousness. Two things, he said, stood out in Davide's character as a jurist. The first was thoroughness: ponencias loaded with relevant detail, fast and avid reading, a day begun at 3:30 a.m. and an arrival at the Court by 6:30 a.m., an elephantine memory that once quoted back footnotes from CJP's own ponencias, and a pen of laser-like precision. The second was moral courage, which he defined as being to a magistrate what political will is to a sovereign head -- the willingness to battle the establishment, to be a beacon for the weak, and to stand by conviction against all odds -- and which he traced to purity of spirit and clarity of conscience. He closed by saying that the guest had not merely challenged the gods but had become the loftiest of the Olympian gods of Padre Faura.
